blocks.text: Gradient accumulation lets a training run achieve the stable gradient dynamics of a large mini-batch, covered in the previous topic, while only ever holding a much smaller mini-batch in memory at any one time, by accumulating gradients across several small steps before actually applying a weight update.

This is one of the most directly useful techniques for fitting a meaningful training run into limited GPU memory, and it complements the QLoRA memory saving techniques covered in the earlier LoRA and QLoRA module.
1. The Problem Gradient Accumulation Solves

blocks.alt: Wanting a large batch runs into not enough memory

blocks.text: A larger mini-batch produces smoother, more stable gradients, but processing a large batch in one step requires holding all of its activations in memory simultaneously, which can exceed what is available, forcing a choice between a smaller batch or a memory upgrade, unless a technique like gradient accumulation is used instead.
2. How Gradient Accumulation Works

blocks.alt: Several mini steps compute gradients, then weights get updated once

blocks.text: Rather than computing gradients and immediately updating weights after one small mini-batch, gradient accumulation runs several small mini-batches in sequence, computing and accumulating their gradients together, and only actually updates the weights once, after all the accumulated steps have contributed.

code.content:
# A simplified gradient accumulation loop
accumulation_steps = 4
optimizer.zero_grad()
for step, mini_batch in enumerate(dataloader):
    predictions = model(mini_batch.inputs)
    loss = compute_loss(predictions, mini_batch.targets) / accumulation_steps
    loss.backward()
    if (step + 1) % accumulation_steps == 0:
        optimizer.step()
        optimizer.zero_grad()

blocks.text: 3. Accumulating Without Updating Yet

blocks.alt: Gradients from each mini step get accumulated but not applied yet

blocks.text: The key mechanism is that gradients from each small step are added together, accumulated, into the same storage, without resetting them between steps, so by the time the weight update finally happens, it reflects the combined gradient signal from every accumulated mini-batch, not just the most recent one.
4. The Effective Batch Size Formula

blocks.alt: Mini-batch size times accumulation steps produces the effective batch size

blocks.text: The effective batch size, the batch size the training dynamics actually behave as if they were using, equals the physical mini-batch size multiplied by the number of accumulation steps, letting a team reach a large effective batch size using only a small amount of memory per individual step.
5. Gradient Accumulation and Memory

blocks.alt: Low memory per step still achieves a large effective batch

blocks.text: Because only one small mini-batch worth of activations needs to be held in memory at any given moment, gradient accumulation keeps peak memory usage low even while achieving the training dynamics of a much larger batch, directly addressing the memory constraint covered in the previous Mini-Batches topic.
6. Gradient Accumulation and Training Speed

blocks.alt: More accumulation steps means slower wall clock time

blocks.text: Gradient accumulation is not free in terms of time, running several small steps before one update takes longer in wall clock time than running one large step would, even though the total amount of computation is roughly the same, a tradeoff worth weighing against the alternative of simply using less memory efficient training.

blocks.title: This is a time for memory tradeoff, not a pure win
blocks.content: Gradient accumulation trades some training speed for memory savings, exactly the same fundamental tradeoff seen in gradient checkpointing, covered in the earlier Training Large Models on Limited GPUs topic.

blocks.text: 7. Choosing an Accumulation Step Count

blocks.alt: A target effective batch divided by the largest mini-batch that fits determines the accumulation steps chosen

blocks.text: A practical way to choose the accumulation step count starts from a target effective batch size, then finds the largest physical mini-batch that actually fits in available memory, and divides the target by that number to determine how many accumulation steps are needed to reach it.
8. Gradient Accumulation vs Just Using a Larger GPU

Gradient accumulation is a software solution to a hardware constraint, when a larger, more capable GPU is genuinely available and affordable, it can simply process a larger batch directly without needing the accumulation workaround, but gradient accumulation remains valuable specifically when that hardware is not available or not cost effective.
9. Common Pitfalls With Gradient Accumulation

A subtle but important detail is dividing the loss by the number of accumulation steps before calling backward, as shown in the earlier code example, without this scaling, the accumulated gradient would end up too large, since it would effectively sum rather than average the loss across the accumulated steps.
Worked Example

A team wants an effective batch size of 32 for stable training dynamics, but their GPU can only fit a physical mini-batch of 4 at a time without running out of memory. Setting accumulation steps to 8 achieves the target effective batch size of 32, at the cost of each weight update now requiring 8 sequential mini steps instead of just 1.

They confirm their loss scaling is correctly dividing by the accumulation step count, avoiding the common pitfall of an inflated accumulated gradient, and their training proceeds with the stability of a batch size of 32 while never exceeding the memory available for a batch size of 4.
Common Mistakes

items: Forgetting to divide the loss by the accumulation step count before calling backward, inflating the accumulated gradient
Calling an optimizer step after every mini step instead of only after the full accumulation cycle completes
Choosing an unnecessarily high accumulation step count, slowing training more than needed for the target effective batch size
Assuming gradient accumulation is entirely free, without accounting for its wall clock time cost

blocks.text: Practice

For a target effective batch size and a maximum physical mini-batch size that fits your available memory, calculate the number of accumulation steps needed to reach that target, confirming the relationship between the three values.
Key Takeaway

Gradient accumulation achieves the stable training dynamics of a large effective batch size while only ever holding a small physical mini-batch in memory at once, accumulating gradients across several small steps before applying one weight update, a time for memory tradeoff that makes large batch training possible even on constrained hardware.
